questions.stem:
Statements:
All cats are animals.
All animals are living beings.
Conclusions:
I. All cats are living beings.
II. Some living beings are cats.
questions.explanation: C is correct. All cats → all animals → all living beings. By transitivity: All cats are living beings (Conclusion I ✓). Since all cats are living beings, those same cats are some living beings that are cats → Some living beings are cats (Conclusion II ✓). Both follow. Method: cats⊂animals⊂living beings (concentric circles). If all A are B and all B are C, then all A are C, and some C are A.

questions.stem:
Statements:
Some books are pens.
All pens are pencils.
Conclusions:
I. Some books are pencils.
II. All pencils are books.
questions.explanation: A is correct. Some books are pens (partial overlap). All pens are pencils. Those pens that are also books become pencils too → Some books are pencils (I ✓). Conclusion II ('All pencils are books') is wrong — pencils can exist that are not books, because the first statement says only SOME books are pens. Diagram: Books circle partially overlaps Pens circle. Pens circle is fully inside Pencils. So some Books are inside Pencils, but not all Pencils are inside Books.

questions.stem:
Statements:
No doctors are lawyers.
All lawyers are teachers.
Conclusions:
I. No teachers are doctors.
II. Some teachers are not doctors.
questions.explanation: B is correct. No doctors are lawyers. All lawyers are teachers → lawyers⊂teachers. Since no doctors are lawyers, those teachers who ARE lawyers are not doctors → Some teachers (the lawyer-teachers) are not doctors (II ✓). Can we say NO teachers are doctors (I)? No — because teachers may include non-lawyer teachers who could be doctors. The statements only exclude lawyer-teachers from being doctors. So I is too strong and does NOT necessarily follow. Only II follows.

questions.stem:
Statements:
All flowers are fruits.
Some fruits are vegetables.
Conclusions:
I. Some flowers are vegetables.
II. Some vegetables are flowers.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Flowers⊂Fruits. Some fruits are vegetables (partial overlap between fruits and vegetables). The overlapping fruits may or may not include any flowers. The statements do not guarantee that the fruits that overlap with vegetables are the same fruits that come from flowers. Diagram: Flowers⊂Fruits; Fruits∩Vegetables≠∅ (some overlap), but the overlap could be entirely in the non-flower part of fruits. Neither I nor II necessarily follows. Trap: Students often assume transitivity when 'some' is involved — but 'some A are B' and 'all C are A' does NOT mean 'some C are B'.

questions.stem:
Statements:
All mangoes are oranges.
No orange is an apple.
Conclusions:
I. No mango is an apple.
II. Some apples are mangoes.
questions.explanation: A is correct. All mangoes are oranges. No orange is an apple. Since no orange is an apple, and all mangoes are oranges, no mango can be an apple (I ✓). Conclusion II ('Some apples are mangoes') directly contradicts I — both cannot follow simultaneously. If no mango is an apple, then no apple is a mango either. II does not follow. Verify: mangoes⊂oranges; oranges∩apples=∅; therefore mangoes∩apples=∅ → No mango is an apple ✓.

questions.stem:
Statements:
Some students are players.
Some players are singers.
Conclusions:
I. Some students are singers.
II. All singers are students.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Some students are players (partial overlap). Some players are singers (partial overlap). The overlapping players may or may not include the student-players. I ('Some students are singers') is not guaranteed — the singer-players might be entirely from the non-student portion of players. II ('All singers are students') is definitely too strong. Neither I nor II necessarily follows. This is the SSC classic 'some-some' trap: two 'some' statements rarely yield a definitive conclusion.

questions.stem:
Statements:
All birds can fly.
A penguin is a bird.
Conclusions:
I. A penguin can fly.
II. Some birds are penguins.
questions.explanation: C is correct. In syllogism questions, we must accept the given statements as true EVEN IF THEY CONTRADICT REAL-WORLD FACTS. The statement 'All birds can fly' is given as universally true. A penguin is a bird → penguin can fly (I ✓). Since penguin is a bird, and penguin is one bird among birds → Some birds are penguins (II ✓). Both follow. SSC syllogism rule: Never use outside knowledge; treat statements as absolute truth for the purpose of the question.

questions.stem:
Statements:
Some tables are chairs.
All chairs are wooden.
Conclusions:
I. All tables are wooden.
II. Some wooden things are tables.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Some tables are chairs. All chairs are wooden → those tables that are chairs are also wooden → Some tables are wooden. But I says 'All tables are wooden' — we only know SOME tables are chairs (and hence wooden); other tables might not be wooden. I does not follow. Since some tables are wooden → some wooden things are tables (II ✓). Only II follows. Verify: tables∩chairs = some overlap; chairs⊂wooden. Overlapping tables are wooden → some tables⊂wooden → some wooden are tables ✓.

questions.stem:
Statements:
No stone is a metal.
All metals are heavy.
Conclusions:
I. No stone is heavy.
II. Some heavy things are not stones.
questions.explanation: B is correct. No stone is a metal. All metals are heavy → metals⊂heavy. Since no stone is a metal, those heavy things that are metals are not stones → Some heavy things (the metals) are not stones (II ✓). Can we say 'No stone is heavy' (I)? No — stones could be heavy for reasons other than being metal. The statement only excludes stones from being metal-type-heavy, not from being heavy in general. Only II follows. This tests the critical reading that absence from one category (metal) doesn't preclude membership in another (heavy).

questions.stem:
Statements:
All roads lead to the city.
Some highways are roads.
Conclusions:
I. Some highways lead to the city.
II. All highways lead to the city.
questions.explanation: A is correct. All roads lead to the city. Some highways are roads → those highways that are roads lead to the city → Some highways lead to the city (I ✓). Conclusion II 'All highways lead to the city' is not established — some highways may not be roads (only SOME highways are roads per the statement). I follows; II does not. Verify: roads⊂city-leading; highways∩roads=some overlap → some highways∩city-leading (I ✓); but highways not fully ⊂ roads → II ✗.
